Description
The Wilson lab in the Department of Entomology at the University of Kentucky is recruiting a PhD student in Entomology to start in Spring 2027. This position will be located in Lexington, Kentucky on the main campus of the University of Kentucky. We study sustainable insect pest management and natural enemy conservation in urban trees, shrubs, and turfgrass. The selected student would be expected to study 1) how flowering lawn weeds influence biological control of scale insects in urban trees, and 2) the degree to which lawn-applied insecticides translocate into scale honeydew in nearby trees and resultant effects on natural enemy communities. The selected student will be encouraged to develop their own research projects under the general themes of the lab.
  Ideal applicants will possess a master’s degree and have a background in entomology, ecology, environmental sciences, biology, or a related field. Exceptional candidates with only a B.S. degree may be considered as well. Prior experience with field-based data collection, scientific writing, and statistical analysis are required. Successful applicants will start in January 2027. Students will receive an assistantship which fully covers tuition and provides a competitive stipend and health insurance. Prospective applicants are encouraged to contact Dr. Caleb Wilson with questions: c.wilson@uky.edu
 The University of Kentucky is located in Lexington, Kentucky which contains a vibrant downtown along with many excellent options for dining, shopping, and outdoor recreation. The department of entomology is composed of 20 faculty with expertise in a wide array of disciplines. The department is consistently ranked as one of the most productive in the country and our students have moved on to successful careers in academia, industry, and government. Starting in December 2026, the department will be based in the newly constructed Agricultural Research Building which will contain state-of-the-art lab equipment for conducting research.
 Additional information can be found at the Wilson lab website: https://caleb-j-wilson.com/, and the University of Kentucky Department of Entomology graduate program: https://entomology.ca.uky.edu/academics/graduate. 
 Prospective students should email application materials to Dr. Caleb Wilson at c.wilson@uky.edu by September 18th, 2026. Interviews will be conducted as applications are received. Applications received after September 18th may still be considered for an interview. The selected candidate will be required to apply to the graduate school at the University of Kentucky by December 1st 2026. Candidates who apply to the graduate school without interviewing with Dr. Wilson will not be considered for this position.
 To apply, please email Dr. Caleb Wilson at c.wilson@uky.edu by September 18th, 2026, with “Scale insect grad student application: First name, Last name” in the subject line and attach the following documents:
1. A cover letter describing research experience, interests, and career goals
2. CV
3. Name and contact information for 3 professional references.
4. An unofficial transcript for all degrees received or in progress.
  Contact
Caleb Wilson
c.wilson@uky.edu (preferred contact method)

Project Description: The Padilla Applied Wildlife Science (PAWS) group at the University of Texas at El Paso (UTEP) is in search of a PhD student to work on population ecology and demographic modeling of an invasive ungulate (Ammotragus lervia) in the Chihuahuan Desert. The student will combine GPS telemetry data, camera trap data, and animal health data to estimate vital rates with the goal of developing population models for aoudad management. This project will include field work at UTEP’s rugged Indio Mountains Research Station along the US-Mexico Border. 
 About me and the lab: The PI - Benjamin Padilla - is an Assistant professor at UTEP with experience working in academia and for the state of Oregon’s Department of Fish and Wildlife. The PAWS group aims to use sound field and quantitative approaches to answer applied questions in wildlife ecology, management and conservation through collaboration, communication, and engagement with stakeholders. 
 About UTEP: UTEP is a Carnegie R1 (very high research activity) university with an active research community and a vibrant campus at the U.S.-Mexico border. El Paso offers unique field access to desert and mountain ecosystems, as well as a dynamic cultural environment that is often a pleasant surprise to first-time visitors.

Description
The Bock Lab (https://samantha-bock.com/) at Oklahoma State University is recruiting two graduate students (MS or PhD) to join the group beginning Fall 2027. We combine approaches from ecology, developmental biology, and comparative genomics to understand how diverse animal life histories emerge and evolve. Graduate students will develop independent projects related to one of the following research areas:
Evolution of temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD) mechanisms in turtles 
Many reptiles rely on temperature to determine offspring sex. This represents a powerful system to examine how developmental processes integrate environmental signals to shape lasting patterns of phenotypic variation. This project will examine the ecological, evolutionary, and genomic processes that shape variation in thermal responses within and across turtle species with TSD. 
Epigenomic drivers of aging and life history variation in sharks & rays
Changes to the epigenome, the layer of chemical modifications that control gene activity and genome stability, are a hallmark of aging and reflect life history variation within and across species. This project will leverage life history variation in elasmobranchs (sharks, skates, and rays) to uncover molecular and evolutionary drivers of variation in aging while also developing non-lethal age markers for use in conservation contexts.

Desired Qualifications
We are seeking enthusiastic, question-driven students with interests in evolutionary ecology, developmental biology, and genomics. Previous experience with bioinformatics is not required, but students with a strong interest in developing these skills are especially encouraged to apply. 
 Funding and Program Information
Students will be supported on a combination of teaching and research assistantships in the Department of Biology at Oklahoma State University. Students are admitted through the Integrative Biology (MS or PhD) graduate program. Program details, stipend information, and admission requirements can be found here: https://cas.okstate.edu/biology/graduate_studies. Additional information about the OSU Graduate College application process can be found here: https://gradcollege.okstate.edu/application-process
 Interested students should email samantha.bock@okstate.edu. In your email please include a CV and brief statement of past research experience and future research interests. Review of materials will occur on a rolling basis beginning immediately and priority will be given to students who submit their materials by September 18, 2026. 
Contact
Samantha Bock
samantha.bock@okstate.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
The Swierk Organismal Ecology Lab in the Department of Biological Sciences at Binghamton University (SUNY) is seeking 1-2 PhD students to join the lab starting Fall 2027 or Spring 2028. Our lab is broadly interested in the function, evolution, and underlying mechanisms of traits associated with animal communication, reproduction, and predator avoidance. We study how selection and phenotypic plasticity shape these traits in heterogeneous environments. Much of our lab’s work is addressed using reptiles (primarily anoles) and amphibians in the Neotropics and in the Northeastern USA. 

The Swierk Lab seeks PhD students who are interested in developing questions that build upon our existing work in either of two research areas: 1) animal body coloration as a dynamic signal in conspecific and heterospecific communication, with an emphasis on visual modeling with respect to animal visual systems; and 2) specialized adaptations facilitating antipredator strategies, specifically the morphology, behavior, and respiratory physiology of rebreathing in semi-aquatic anoles. These projects will be developed using Neotropical anoles as a study system. 

Qualifications: 
BA/BS in related field 
Motivated, independent, collaborative 
Relevant research experience 
Demonstrated scientific writing and communication skills 
Willing to spend 2-3 summer months/year conducting research at Neotropical field stations 

Preferred candidates will also have: 
Strong statistical / quantitative skills 
Prior experience with tropical field research, animal behavior, and/or herpetology 
Completion of MS degree (though any candidate is welcome to apply)
Interest in applying for external grants/fellowships (e.g., NSF GRFP) 

Binghamton University (BU) is the top-ranked institution in the SUNY system and is consistently rated as one of the premier public universities in the Northeast. BU is included in the Carnegie Classification system's "very high research activity" (R1) category. PhD students are supported by tuition-waived teaching assistantships. Our 930-acre campus is located in the Southern Tier of New York, between the Catskills and Finger Lakes, about a 3-hour drive from NYC. The region features abundant opportunities for outdoor recreation and a very reasonable cost of living. 

To indicate interest: Please email LSwierk@binghamton.edu with a subject line “Prospective PhD 2027”. In the email, please include which of the two research areas (outlined above) you are interested in, a brief description of past research experience, your GPA and relevant coursework, and your CV with references. You may also send reprints of published papers or writing samples, if you wish. Qualified applicants will later be invited to send in a formal application to BU’s Graduate School. 

Contact
Dr. Lindsey Swierk
lswierk@binghamton.edu (preferred contact method)

Project Description
We seek an outstanding student to pursue a PhD research project to advance the study of white-tailed deer health and disease ecology in partnership with Bemidji State University and the Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa (FDL Band). Waawaashkeshi (white-tailed deer) are a species of social, cultural, and economic importance to the FDL Band as well as to non-tribal members within the region. The Fond du Lac Reservation and surrounding 1854 Ceded Territory are broadly representative of habitats, ecosystems, and deer hunting culture found throughout much of northern Minnesota. It is also an area proposed for the reintroduction of elk. This research is focused on understanding deer population health dynamics and its association with deer management and survival. Health data generated from this research will be used to conduct a disease risk analysis to clearly identify and prioritize disease hazards to mitigate during the potential translocation of elk. The collaborative project will involve a substantial amount of field work (which the student will plan and implement), data collection and management, laboratory activities, and advanced epidemiological and ecological modeling. 

Requirements and Qualifications
·       BS in wildlife biology, ecology, or related field. 
·       Strong work ethic; excellent oral and written communication skills, high attention to detail; the ability to work independently and with external partners; and deep respect for indigenous sovereignty and dedication to cultivating respectful partnerships with indigenous communities in research. 
·       A positive attitude and the personality to work/live amicably with others will also be an advantage. 
·       Willingness and ability to work long hours in the field in extreme weather conditions. 
·       Preference will be given to candidates with Native American heritage. 

More information?
·       Check out the University of Minnesota Conservation Sciences Program.  
·       To apply, a formal application package must be submitted at Slate and includes 1) a cover letter that highlights experiences and interest in graduate training, 2) your CV/resume, 3) your unofficial transcripts, and 4) 3 references. Application deadline is November 30, 2026.  Please contact Dr. Tiffany Wolf at wolfx305@umn.edu for additional questions regarding this opportunity.

Project: Drs. Brittany Mosher (Wildlife Ecology Research Lab) and Mark Henderson (Henderson Lab) at The University of Vermont’s Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources are seeking a master’s-level graduate student to participate in research related to the movement of Spiny Softshells (Apalone spinifera) in Lake Champlain. The position is available beginning in either January or June 2027 and includes two years of funding (stipend, tuition waiver, and health insurance) in the form of both a graduate research assistantship and a graduate teaching assistantship. The student will be co-mentored by Dr. Brittany Mosher (UVM), Dr. Mark Henderson (USGS), and Dr. Luke Groff (Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department).
 Project description: The Spiny Softshell is threatened and a Species of Greatest Conservation Need in Vermont and is endangered in Quebec. Native populations of Spiny Softshells are not found elsewhere in the northeastern US. In Vermont, the species has been listed as threatened since 1987 due to shoreline habitat destruction, the rarity of suitable nesting beaches, and small adult population sizes. Spiny softshell reports primarily come from northern Lake Champlain near the mouth of the Lamoille River, in Missisquoi Bay, and recently, near the mouth of the Winooski River. It is unknown whether these three areas represent distinct subpopulations or whether they are connected. Our limited knowledge about population interchange and movement patterns impedes Spiny Softshell management and recovery decision-making. 
 This project will use the existing Champlain Acoustic Telemetry Observation System (CATOS) to understand Spiny Softshell movement patterns and population connectivity in Lake Champlain and its tributaries. The objectives of this research project are to: 1) Determine whether there is interchange between Vermont’s Spiny Softshell populations. 2) Identify Spiny Softshell movement corridors and barriers. 3) Assess whether the Spiny Softshell has recolonized the Winooski River. 4) Share research findings with K-12 students and with local partners.

Applicants should have a strong work ethic, experience working as part of a field crew, and a strong interest in data analysis and scientific writing. Training will be provided, but experience working with large and/or spatial ecological datasets (e.g., in R), as well as familiarity with capture methods for freshwater turtle species are highly desirable. The two missions of the PGRU are the preservation of germplasm of selected crop plants and the breeding and improvement of apples.  Specific activities include acquisition, documentation, maintenance, characterization, breeding, enhancement and distribution of the assigned crops. USDA plant germplasm collections

 Responsibilities and tasks: Procambarus clarkii (Red Swamp Crawfish) are simultaneously desired as an aquaculture product and reviled as an invasive species worldwide. Aquaculture practices to efficiently produce crayfish while minimizing risk of escapement and establishment of invasive populations are urgently needed. The successful candidate(s) will join a collaborative project involving Auburn University (USA), Ben Gurion University (Israel) and the USGS to develop techniques for efficient crayfish production in indoor recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS), investigate genetic and physiological mechanisms controlling sexual development, and produce neofemales (genetic males that develop into functional females) for production of all-male broods and invasive species control. Description
Position Overview

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) invites applications for a Postdoctoral Research Associate to join an interdisciplinary research project investigating avian migration in the Intermountain West with large-scale bioacoustics approaches. This is a full-time appointment for one year with anticipated renewal for a second year, contingent on funding and job performance.

The postdoctoral researcher will play a leading role in analyzing an extensive acoustic dataset of migratory birds in western North America. The project integrates bioacoustic monitoring, machine learning-based species classification, landscape ecology, and weather and radar data to address fundamental and applied questions about bird migration. The position offers opportunities to lead multiple peer-reviewed publications and to collaborate with researchers at UIUC, MPG Ranch, and partner institutions. The postdoctoral researcher will be primarily supervised by Dr. Benjamin Van Doren, Assistant Professor in the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences (https://www.migrationbiology.org/).

Research Focus

This research will apply recent advances in AI-enabled bioacoustic analysis to a multi-year archive of passive acoustic recordings collected across a network of sites in the Intermountain West. The postdoctoral researcher will contribute to research aims that will include (1) landscape influences on migratory habitat use and (2) environmental drivers of migration decision-making. There may also be opportunities to pursue project extensions, such as incorporating additional acoustic datasets, modeling fine-scale migration flows, examining social dynamics of migrants, analyzing regional variation in vocalizations, or linking bioacoustic data with large-scale monitoring programs.

Responsibilities

Lead quantitative analyses of large-scale bioacoustic, environmental, and landscape datasets
Integrate acoustic data with radar, weather, and remote-sensing products
Develop and publish peer-reviewed manuscripts (expected 3–4 papers over the appointment)
Contribute to project coordination with research partners
Mentor graduate and undergraduate students 
Present findings at scientific conferences and workshops

Required Qualifications

Ph.D. in Ecology, Wildlife Biology, Conservation Biology, Computational Biology, or a related field 
Strong quantitative and analytical skills
Experience working with large ecological datasets
Proficiency in R and/or Python for data analysis
Demonstrated ability to lead scientific publications

Preferred Qualifications

Experience with bioacoustics, passive acoustic monitoring, or automated species classification
Familiarity with bird migration ecology
Experience integrating ecological data with weather, radar, or remote-sensing data
Background in spatial or landscape ecology
Interest in applied conservation questions

Salary and Benefits

The anticipated salary range is $55,000–$60,000, commensurate with experience. The position includes a comprehensive benefits package.

Remote Work Policy

Candidates able to work in person at UIUC will be preferred, but hybrid and remote work arrangements may be considered. 

University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

UIUC is a leading public research university with a strong tradition of interdisciplinary scholarship. The campus hosts world-class programs in ecology, evolutionary biology, natural resources, computer science, and data science, providing a rich intellectual environment for collaborative research. Champaign-Urbana offers a high quality of life, a low cost of living, and a vibrant academic community.

Application Instructions

Applicants should submit the following documents to the form located at https://forms.gle/nRT7gXgsB5sASDuW8.

A cover letter describing research interests, relevant experience, and interest in this position
A curriculum vitae (CV)
Contact information for 3 references
